memories.line: Every box has a number. I gave my cat a number once. She did not answer to it.
Your dispatch has a number now. Someone will look it up in fifty years. Write for them.
I copy all day. My hand knows the words better than my head. That is the danger.
Since your dispatch, people ask me which copy came first. Nobody asked that in years.
The scribes wrote about the workers. No worker wrote here. I keep one chair empty for them.
You left room in the record for the people who did not write it. My empty chair has company now.
Roads. Crates. Sand. I build them small, so I can be wrong cheaply.
Your crate went by the road you chose. My model was wrong about the dust. Good. Now I know.
A file with a gap keeps me awake. I count the pages twice before bed.
You put the gap on the heading. I slept badly. Then, for the first time in years, I slept well.
Kings kept fine records of kings. Ask me who kept records of the cooks.
A woman with a gold stamp asked me to call the file complete. I told her what you would tell her.
Fog comes in at noon here. The site files smell of salt. So do I.
You kept the two records side by side. Families stand between them a long time.
Today's questions: where is the tea, are they real, and why is a cat on my desk. I can answer one.
Visitors read your heading out loud. The children read the gap part loudest.
Wind's backing west. Three flags if it holds. Two if it lies.
The boats came in. Some fishers grumbled about the warning. Let them grumble on dry land.
I wrote 'seventy in a hundred'. The harbour heard 'it will rain'. Where did my thirty go?
After your notice, a fisher asked me what 'perhaps' means. Nobody ever asked me that.
Shh. If you can hear the creek, the birds can hear you.
You corrected your notice in front of everyone. The crews trust it more now, not less. Strange creatures, people.
Two bridges, one crew, and a bird count that changes by the hour. Pick a number and stand by it.
Your count kept a blank where the creek was blocked. I would have filled it in. You were right not to.
Zero the balance. Zero it again. The day I skip that is the day it lies.
Someone brought me a Seal-stamped ingot. I weighed the stamp. It weighs nothing.
Hesper's grandmother? Oh, there are stories, dear. And there is a ledger. They do not agree.
Your docket is in the ledger now. I underlined your name. Twice. Do not tell the Inspector.
Ink on my hands, ink on my lunch. A copy is only as good as the tired person who sets it.
The Nexus once dropped a caveat from a reprint, they say. We laughed about it for years. I am not laughing now.
A missing Tuesday means old Ama walked here in the rain for nothing. A notice is not just paper.
Ama came on the right day this week. She brought me a pear. Really, it is your pear.
A blank on a chart is not a failure. It is the most honest ink I own.
The skiff slowed down at your blank. The skipper cursed. Then she thanked me.
The survey says 'Point C'. My grandmother says 'Where-the-Gulls-Argue'. Only one name tells you to slow down.
Your key kept our names. The children read the chart now, and argue with it. Good.
Silence is a prop, darling. The most expensive one we have.
That rival of yours sat in row three and bowed at the end. Lovely posture. Some terrible ideas. Not all.
From the side seats you see the stagehand. From the front, you see magic. Same show.
People asked what they could see from their own seat. Twelve years I have worked here. That never happened before.
Basket in, basket out. You would be amazed what a basket weighs when nobody is looking.
Seal agents came with a gold stamp for my balance. I told them my balance does not need jewellery.
Price per measure! My favourite words. I made a chart. I make charts when I am nervous.
Households ask for the price per measure now. I made another chart. I am very proud of this one.
My mother kept a weir in a town that is not on the maps now. Gates remember floods. People forget.
You found the old order with the Nexus mark. I knew the name of that town. I did not say it. I am sorry.
Rule seven: water follows the order. Rule eight: the order follows the water, when they disagree.
Your plan shows who loses in a drought. The council hated that. Then they used it.
The machine is fair. It treats every request the same. Why are you looking at me like that?
The machine missed Canal Walk for two years. Same rule, every day. Fair, and never looking up.
Seventeen complaints, one notice board, no pins. Welcome to public service.
Canal Walk has a library stop now. Someone left flowers on my board. Nobody leaves flowers on a board.
A voice remembers how. A record remembers when. I need both, and I rarely get both.
There is a recording here in Elsbet's voice. I kept it for ten years. I think it was waiting for you.
Lantern four or lantern six? Everyone remembers the walk. Nobody remembers the date.
Your notice keeps the memory and the record on their own lines. The old walkers feel heard, and checked.
Eight crates, three routes, one ferry. Every model is wrong. Some are useful before lunch.
Your rival helped with the plan? On my island? I need to sit down.
Smaller landing, smaller loads. The sea does not read your plan.
The crates came. The fair has its apples. I will say it once: good plan.
Three watches say noon. One is right, or none. Time is a promise that people agree to keep.
You carried a little brass lamp into the Council. I have mended every lamp in this hall. Never that one.
The rail was repaired on a date. The record says so. The repairer wrote the record. You see my problem.
Whatever the Council decided, it decided in the open. The bell rang on time today. Coincidence, probably.
